questions.question: You need to deploy a stateless web application that automatically scales from 0 to millions of requests with no infrastructure management. Which GCP compute service is the best fit?
options: Compute Engine MIGs
GKE Standard mode
Cloud Run
App Engine Flex
questions.explanation: Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform that automatically scales containers from 0 to N based on incoming requests. It requires zero infrastructure management and is ideal for stateless workloads. App Engine Flexible and GKE require more configuration; Compute Engine MIGs need autoscaler setup.

questions.question: A developer needs to grant a service account the minimum permissions to read objects from a specific Cloud Storage bucket. Which IAM role should be granted at the bucket level?
options: roles/storage.objectAdmin
roles/storage.objectViewer
roles/storage.bucketReader
roles/storage.objectCreator
questions.explanation: roles/storage.objectViewer grants read access to objects within a bucket (storage.objects.get and storage.objects.list) without bucket-level administrative permissions, satisfying least privilege. roles/storage.objectAdmin permits write and delete on objects; roles/storage.bucketReader grants metadata read on the bucket itself; roles/storage.objectCreator allows uploads only.

questions.question: You are creating a VM instance that needs to access BigQuery and Cloud Storage without storing credentials on disk. What is the recommended approach?
options: Copy a service account JSON key onto the VM disk
Set credentials in startup-script env variables
Attach a service account to the VM instance
Use the default compute SA with Editor role
questions.explanation: Attaching a service account to a VM instance allows workloads to authenticate to Google Cloud APIs using the service account's identity via the metadata server — no key files needed. Storing key files on disk is a security risk. The default service account with Editor is overly permissive. Environment variables are not a secure long-term solution.

questions.question: Which Cloud Storage storage class should you use for data that is accessed at most once a year and requires 99.9% availability?
options: Standard
Nearline
Coldline
Archive
questions.explanation: Coldline is designed for data accessed at most once per 90 days (roughly quarterly or less). For once-a-year access, Coldline is appropriate and cost-effective. Archive is for data accessed less than once per year with a 365-day minimum storage duration. Nearline is for monthly access. Standard is for frequently accessed data.

questions.question: You need to allow traffic from the internet to reach VMs on port 443 in your VPC. No current firewall rule exists. What must you do?
options: Configure a VPC peering connection from the public internet
Create an ingress firewall rule allowing TCP:443 from 0.0.0.0/0
Assign an external IP to each VM and enable forwarding
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway for inbound HTTPS traffic
questions.explanation: GCP VPCs use an implicit deny-all ingress rule by default. You must create an explicit ingress firewall rule allowing TCP port 443 from source 0.0.0.0/0 (internet). External IPs alone don't open firewall ports. Cloud NAT is for outbound connectivity. VPC peering connects private networks.

questions.question: Your GKE cluster needs to run a DaemonSet that collects logs from every node. What is the correct Kubernetes resource to deploy?
options: Deployment with replicas=node count
StatefulSet with anti-affinity
DaemonSet
CronJob with hostNetwork
questions.explanation: A DaemonSet ensures that exactly one pod replica runs on every node (or a subset defined by node selectors). This is the standard pattern for log collectors, monitoring agents, and network plugins. Deployments and StatefulSets don't guarantee one-pod-per-node. CronJobs are for scheduled batch tasks.

questions.question: Which gcloud command lists all Compute Engine instances in a specific project and zone?
options: gcloud compute instances describe --zone=us-central1-a
gcloud compute instances list --zone=us-central1-a
gcloud compute instances list --region=us-central1-a
gcloud compute vms list --zone=us-central1-a
questions.explanation: gcloud compute instances list --zone=ZONE lists all VM instances in that zone. The describe subcommand shows details of a single named instance. The other options use incorrect command syntax.

questions.question: You need a fully managed relational database compatible with MySQL 8.0 on GCP. Which service should you use?
options: Cloud Bigtable
Cloud Spanner
Cloud SQL
Firestore
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL is Google's fully managed relational database service supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. Cloud Bigtable is a NoSQL wide-column store. Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database for massive scale. Firestore is a NoSQL document database.

questions.question: A team wants to monitor the CPU utilization of their Compute Engine VMs and be alerted when it exceeds 80% for more than 5 minutes. What should they use?
options: Cloud Audit Logs with notification channels
Cloud Monitoring with an alerting policy
Cloud Trace with custom span alerting
Error Reporting with email subscriptions
questions.explanation: Cloud Monitoring (formerly Stackdriver) collects metrics from GCP resources and allows you to define alerting policies with conditions, notification channels, and duration thresholds. Cloud Audit Logs track API activity. Cloud Trace analyzes request latency. Error Reporting aggregates application errors.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Cloud NAT gateway in GCP?
options: Provides inbound load balancing for VMs without external IP addresses
Lets VMs without external IPs initiate outbound internet connections
Peers two VPCs across regions and projects in the same organization
Encrypts traffic between on-premises networks and Google Cloud VPCs
questions.explanation: Cloud NAT (Network Address Translation) allows VM instances without external IP addresses to make outbound connections to the internet while hiding their internal IPs. It does not allow unsolicited inbound connections. VPC peering is a separate service; Cloud VPN/Interconnect handles on-premises encryption.

questions.question: You need to deploy a containerized application that requires persistent disk storage and must maintain a stable network identity. Which GCP/Kubernetes resource is most appropriate?
options: Deployment with a PersistentVolumeClaim
StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates
DaemonSet with hostPath volume mounts
ReplicaSet with an external LoadBalancer
questions.explanation: StatefulSets provide stable network identities (predictable pod names), ordered deployment/scaling, and per-pod persistent storage via volumeClaimTemplates. This is the correct choice for databases and stateful applications. Deployments support PVCs but don't provide stable pod identities.

questions.question: Which load balancer type should you choose to route HTTP/HTTPS traffic globally to backends in multiple regions with built-in DDoS protection?
options: Internal TCP/UDP Load Balancer (regional)
Regional External TCP/UDP Load Balancer
Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer
Internal HTTP(S) Load Balancer (regional)
questions.explanation: The Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer is a Layer 7 proxy that uses Google's global network to route requests to the nearest healthy backend. It includes Cloud Armor for DDoS protection and supports URL-based routing. Internal load balancers are for private traffic. Regional load balancers don't offer global routing.

questions.question: A project has multiple environments (dev, staging, prod). What is the recommended GCP resource hierarchy approach to isolate billing and access control per environment?
options: Use separate VPCs within the same shared project
Use separate GCP projects for each environment
Use separate service accounts in one shared project
Use labels and folders to tag resources by env
questions.explanation: GCP's resource hierarchy uses projects as the primary unit of isolation. Separate projects provide independent billing, IAM policies, quotas, and audit trails per environment. VPC separation and labels don't provide billing or IAM isolation. Service accounts within one project still share project-level IAM policies.

questions.question: You need to store structured, schemaless JSON documents with real-time sync for a mobile application. Which GCP database is the best fit?
options: Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL)
Cloud Bigtable
Firestore
Cloud Spanner
questions.explanation: Firestore (formerly Cloud Firestore/Datastore) is Google's serverless NoSQL document database with real-time sync, offline support, and automatic scaling — purpose-built for mobile and web applications. Cloud Bigtable is for time-series/analytics at massive scale. Cloud SQL/Spanner are relational databases.

questions.question: What happens to data in a Cloud Storage bucket when you enable Versioning?
options: The latest version overwrites the previous one with no history retained
Each update creates a new version; prior versions are retained with a generation ID
Objects are replicated to additional regions for read availability and durability
Objects are placed under a retention lock until the lifecycle policy releases them
questions.explanation: Cloud Storage Versioning maintains every version of an object. When an object is overwritten or deleted, the old version is retained with its original generation number. You can restore, list, or permanently delete non-current versions. Versioning does not affect replication settings or make objects immutable by default.

questions.question: You need to schedule a Bash script to run every day at 2 AM on GCP with no persistent VM. What is the most cost-effective approach?
options: Keep a Compute Engine VM running 24/7 with a crontab entry for the job
Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Function or Cloud Run job
Run a GKE CronJob on a small autoscaling node pool for the schedule
Deploy an App Engine Standard service with the cron.yaml scheduler
questions.explanation: Cloud Scheduler + Cloud Functions or Cloud Run is the serverless, cost-effective pattern for scheduled tasks. You pay only for execution time. A 24/7 VM is wasteful for a once-daily task. GKE has minimum cluster costs. App Engine scheduled tasks work but are less flexible and cost more.

questions.question: A GKE cluster's nodes are running out of memory. You want the cluster to automatically add more nodes when resource utilization is high. What should you enable?
options: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
Cluster Autoscaler
Vertical Pod Autoscaler
Node Auto-Provisioning
questions.explanation: Cluster Autoscaler automatically adds or removes nodes based on pending pod scheduling requirements and resource utilization. HPA scales the number of pod replicas, not nodes. VPA adjusts resource requests for individual pods. Node auto-provisioning creates new node pools when needed, but Cluster Autoscaler is the primary node-scaling mechanism.

questions.question: Which command creates a new Kubernetes namespace called 'production' in your current GKE cluster context?
options: gcloud container namespaces create production
kubectl create namespace production
kubectl create ns production --type=v1
gcloud kubernetes namespace add production
questions.explanation: kubectl create namespace production is the correct Kubernetes CLI command to create a namespace. GCP's gcloud tool doesn't have a direct namespace management command — namespaces are Kubernetes API objects managed via kubectl.

questions.question: You need to connect your on-premises network to a GCP VPC with dedicated bandwidth of 10 Gbps and low latency. SLAs are critical. Which connectivity option should you choose?
options: Cloud VPN over the public internet
Dedicated Interconnect with a colo
Partner Interconnect via a carrier
Cloud NAT with private routing
questions.explanation: Dedicated Interconnect provides a direct physical connection between your on-premises network and Google's network, offering 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps links with 99.99% SLA when configured with redundancy. Cloud VPN uses the public internet with lower bandwidth. Partner Interconnect uses a service provider. Cloud NAT is for outbound internet access.

questions.question: Which IAM binding allows you to grant a role to all users of your Google Workspace domain?
options: allUsers (the public IAM identifier)
allAuthenticatedUsers (Google IAM)
domain:yourdomain.com (Workspace)
group:everyone@yourdomain.com
questions.explanation: The domain: principal type grants access to all Google accounts in a Google Workspace (or Cloud Identity) domain. 'allUsers' grants access to everyone on the internet (unauthenticated included). 'allAuthenticatedUsers' covers all Google-signed-in users globally. group: requires a specific Google Group.

questions.question: You deployed a Cloud Run service and need to split traffic so that 90% goes to revision v2 and 10% goes to revision v1 for canary testing. How do you configure this?
options: Use a global HTTP(S) Load Balancer with weighted backends
Configure traffic splitting in Cloud Run service settings
Deploy two separate Cloud Run services behind a load balancer
Use Cloud CDN to route a percentage of traffic per revision
questions.explanation: Cloud Run natively supports traffic splitting between revisions. You can assign percentage weights to each revision (e.g., 90% to v2, 10% to v1) directly in the Cloud Run service configuration. This is a built-in canary deployment feature requiring no additional infrastructure.

questions.question: Your application running on Compute Engine is writing logs. Where should you direct logs so they are automatically ingested into Cloud Logging?
options: Write logs to /var/log/syslog — they are ingested automatically
Install and configure the Cloud Logging agent (Ops Agent) on the VM
Compute Engine streams system logs without any agent installation
Write logs to a Cloud Storage bucket and import them on a schedule
questions.explanation: Compute Engine VMs do not automatically stream application/system logs. You must install the Ops Agent (or legacy Logging agent), which collects and forwards logs to Cloud Logging. The Ops Agent also collects metrics. GCP-managed services like GKE and App Engine auto-send logs without an agent.

questions.question: A Cloud SQL instance is experiencing high read latency under heavy load. You want to offload read queries without changing the application architecture significantly. What should you add?
options: Upgrade the Cloud SQL tier to a larger machine
Add a read replica to the Cloud SQL instance
Add Memorystore for Redis as a read-through cache
Migrate the workload to Cloud Spanner for scale-out
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL read replicas are asynchronous copies of the primary instance that serve read-only queries, offloading traffic without requiring application changes (just point read queries to the replica endpoint). Scaling up the instance tier helps but is more expensive. Memorystore helps but requires application-level cache logic. Spanner is a major migration.

questions.question: You need to ensure a Cloud Storage bucket can only be accessed from within a specific VPC network. What feature should you configure?
options: Bucket-level IAM allow policy
VPC Service Controls
Uniform bucket-level access
Cloud Armor security policy
questions.explanation: VPC Service Controls create a security perimeter around GCP services (including Cloud Storage) that restricts access to requests originating from authorized VPC networks or IP ranges. IAM policies control who can access resources but not from where. Cloud Armor protects HTTP(S) Load Balancers. Uniform bucket-level access standardizes ACLs.

questions.question: Your GKE workload requires access to a Cloud SQL database. What is the recommended, secure way to provide credentials?
options: Hardcode the database password in the Deployment YAML manifest
Store credentials in a Kubernetes Secret mounted as an env variable
Use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy with Workload Identity bindings
Grant the cluster's default service account the Editor IAM role
questions.explanation: The recommended pattern is Cloud SQL Auth Proxy (runs as a sidecar or standalone) combined with Workload Identity, which maps a Kubernetes Service Account to a GCP Service Account. The proxy handles encrypted connections and IAM authentication — no passwords are stored. Kubernetes Secrets in plain YAML are base64-encoded but not encrypted at rest by default.

questions.question: Which pricing model for Compute Engine provides up to 57% discount automatically for instances that run for a significant portion of the billing month, with no upfront commitment?
options: Committed Use Discounts (1 or 3-year)
Preemptible VMs (legacy short-lived)
Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs)
Spot VMs (interruption-tolerant)
questions.explanation: Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs) are automatic discounts applied when a Compute Engine resource runs for more than 25% of a month. The discount increases incrementally up to ~57% for full-month use with no action required. CUDs require 1- or 3-year commitments. Preemptible/Spot VMs are discounted but can be interrupted.

questions.question: You need to deploy an application to App Engine Standard. The application receives bursts of traffic and must scale to zero when idle. Which App Engine environment should you choose?
options: App Engine Flexible with automatic scaling
App Engine Standard with automatic scaling
App Engine Standard with manual scaling
App Engine Flexible with manual scaling
questions.explanation: App Engine Standard with automatic scaling can scale to zero instances when there's no traffic, meaning no cost during idle periods. App Engine Flexible environments run at minimum one instance (cannot scale to zero). Manual scaling doesn't scale automatically.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Google Cloud's Organization Policy Service?
options: Defines IAM roles for users and groups across the organization
Enforces configuration constraints on GCP resources across the org
Monitors API and quota usage across the projects in the org
Manages billing accounts, budgets, and alerts for the organization
questions.explanation: Organization Policy Service lets you set constraints on how GCP resources can be configured — for example, preventing public IP addresses on VMs, enforcing specific regions, or disabling service account key creation. These policies apply at the organization, folder, or project level and override individual IAM permissions.

questions.question: A VM instance has been accidentally deleted. You had taken a snapshot of its boot disk 2 hours before. How do you restore the VM?
options: Restore directly from the snapshot — it re-creates the original VM
Create a new disk from the snapshot, then create a VM using that disk
Use Cloud Backup and DR to restore the VM state from the snapshot
Snapshots are diagnostic artifacts and unsuitable for VM recovery
questions.explanation: To restore from a snapshot: (1) create a new persistent disk from the snapshot, (2) create a new VM instance using that disk as the boot disk. Snapshots are disk images, not full VM backups — they don't automatically recreate a VM. You'll need to reconfigure any VM-specific settings (network, labels, etc.).

questions.question: You want to analyze structured log data stored in Cloud Logging using SQL queries. What is the best approach?
options: Use Cloud Monitoring's Metrics Explorer to write SQL queries on logs
Export logs to BigQuery using a log sink, then query them with SQL
Use Cloud Trace to query structured log payloads with a SQL dialect
Query the logs directly in Cloud Logging using a BigQuery SQL syntax
questions.explanation: Log sinks allow you to route log entries to destinations like BigQuery, Cloud Storage, or Pub/Sub. Exporting to BigQuery lets you run full SQL analytics on log data at scale. Cloud Logging's query language (Log Analytics) does support SQL-like queries now, but for complex analytics BigQuery is the standard pattern.

questions.question: Which GCP service provides a globally distributed, strongly consistent relational database that automatically scales horizontally across regions?
options: Cloud SQL HA configuration
Cloud Bigtable
Cloud Spanner
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner is Google's proprietary globally distributed relational database providing ACID transactions, strong consistency, and horizontal scalability across regions — something no traditional relational database can do. Cloud SQL is regionally bound. Bigtable is NoSQL. AlloyDB is a high-performance PostgreSQL-compatible service but not globally distributed.

questions.question: You need to give an external auditor read-only access to Cloud Logging audit logs in your project. Which predefined IAM role is most appropriate?
options: roles/logging.admin (full logging)
roles/logging.privateLogViewer
roles/logging.viewer (standard)
roles/viewer (project-wide read)
questions.explanation: roles/logging.privateLogViewer grants access to all logs including data access audit logs (which are considered sensitive/private). roles/logging.viewer only shows non-private logs. roles/viewer is a broad project-level role. roles/logging.admin has full control. For an auditor needing access to audit logs, privateLogViewer is the correct minimum role.

questions.question: Your Cloud Storage bucket needs a policy that automatically deletes objects older than 30 days. What should you configure?
options: A Cloud Scheduler job that calls the Storage API daily
Object Lifecycle Management rules on the bucket
A Cloud Function triggered by object creation events
Retention policies on the bucket and object hold
questions.explanation: Object Lifecycle Management lets you define rules to automatically transition or delete objects based on age, version count, storage class, or other conditions. Setting an Age condition of 30 days with a Delete action is the built-in, zero-code solution. Retention policies actually prevent deletion. Scheduler + Function adds unnecessary complexity.

questions.question: What does enabling 'uniform bucket-level access' on a Cloud Storage bucket do?
options: Replicates the bucket's contents across multiple GCP regions
Disables object-level ACLs and enforces IAM-only access control
Enables object versioning automatically for all uploads to the bucket
Encrypts every object with a customer-managed key in Cloud KMS
questions.explanation: Uniform bucket-level access (UBA) disables legacy object-level ACLs and enforces that access is controlled entirely by Cloud IAM. This simplifies permission management (one system instead of two) and is required for some compliance frameworks. It does not affect replication, versioning, or encryption.

questions.question: You need to set up a budget alert that notifies the billing admin when spending reaches 80% of the monthly budget. What GCP service handles this?
options: Cloud Monitoring with a custom metric alert
Cloud Billing budgets and alerts
Cloud Pub/Sub billing event topic
Looker Studio billing dashboard alert
questions.explanation: Cloud Billing budgets allow you to define a spending threshold and configure alerts at specific percentages (e.g., 50%, 80%, 100%) that send email notifications or Pub/Sub messages. This is the native GCP billing alert mechanism. Cloud Monitoring handles performance metrics, not billing thresholds.

questions.question: A microservices application running on GKE needs service-to-service communication with mTLS encryption and traffic policies without modifying application code. What should you deploy?
options: Cloud Endpoints API gateway service
Anthos Service Mesh (built on Istio)
Cloud Armor security policies on pods
Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) with GKE
questions.explanation: Istio / Anthos Service Mesh implements a sidecar proxy model that transparently adds mTLS encryption, traffic management (canary, circuit breaker, retries), and observability to service-to-service communication without changing application code. IAP authenticates users. Cloud Endpoints manages APIs. Cloud Armor protects load balancers.

questions.question: You need to give a VM in Project A access to a Cloud Storage bucket in Project B. What is the correct approach?
options: Cross-project access is blocked by default — request a quota change
Share the Project A owner credentials with the Project B service account
Grant the VM's SA the right IAM role on the bucket in Project B
Establish VPC Network Peering between Project A and Project B networks
questions.explanation: IAM roles can be granted to any principal (including service accounts from other projects) on any resource. Grant the service account attached to the Project A VM the required role (e.g., roles/storage.objectViewer) on the specific bucket in Project B. Cross-project access via service accounts is a standard GCP pattern.

questions.question: Which Compute Engine feature lets you run fault-tolerant batch workloads at up to 91% discount, accepting that VMs may be preempted?
options: Committed Use Discounts
Custom machine types
Spot VMs (Preemptible)
Sole-tenant nodes
questions.explanation: Spot VMs (the current name, replacing Preemptible VMs) offer up to 91% discount over on-demand pricing. They can be preempted with 30-second notice when Compute Engine needs capacity. They are ideal for batch processing, rendering, and fault-tolerant distributed workloads that can checkpoint progress.

questions.question: A new GCP project needs to use the Pub/Sub API. What must you do before making API calls?
options: Pub/Sub becomes available once the project is created and billed
Open a support ticket to have Google Cloud enable the Pub/Sub API
Enable the Pub/Sub API in the project via Cloud Console or gcloud
Create a Pub/Sub service account first and the API auto-activates
questions.explanation: Most GCP APIs are disabled by default in new projects. You must explicitly enable each API you want to use (via Cloud Console > APIs & Services > Enable APIs, or gcloud services enable pubsub.googleapis.com). Service account creation doesn't auto-enable APIs.

questions.question: You need to deploy infrastructure across multiple GCP projects using repeatable, version-controlled configuration. Which tool is most appropriate?
options: Cloud Deployment Manager templates
gcloud scripts in Source Repositories
Terraform with GCP provider
Cloud Build pipelines
questions.explanation: Terraform is the industry-standard IaC tool for GCP (and multi-cloud), supporting state management, plan/apply workflows, modules, and version control integration. Cloud Deployment Manager is GCP-native but less feature-rich and not multi-cloud. gcloud scripts are procedural, not declarative. Cloud Build is a CI/CD service.

questions.question: Which GCP service provides a fully managed Apache Kafka-compatible message streaming platform?
options: Cloud Tasks queue
Cloud Pub/Sub
Datastream CDC
Pub/Sub Lite
questions.explanation: Cloud Pub/Sub is Google's fully managed messaging service. While not strictly Kafka-compatible in protocol, it serves the same architectural role and now offers Pub/Sub Lite for higher-throughput lower-cost streaming. For native Kafka protocol compatibility, Confluent on GCP or Managed Kafka is used. In the ACE exam context, Pub/Sub is the GCP-native streaming answer.

questions.question: What does a GCP 'folder' in the resource hierarchy provide that a project alone cannot?
options: Provides each folder with its own billing account and quota pool
Groups projects so IAM and Org Policies inherit down the hierarchy
Creates network isolation boundaries between the projects inside it
Is required to activate certain Google Cloud services in the projects
questions.explanation: Folders in GCP's resource hierarchy (Organization > Folders > Projects > Resources) allow you to group projects by department or environment and apply IAM bindings and Organization Policies at the folder level. These policies inherit down to all child projects. Billing is managed at the project level. Folders don't create network isolation.

questions.question: You need to encrypt a Cloud SQL database with a key that your team manages and can rotate. Which encryption option should you use?
options: Google-managed encryption keys (default GMEK)
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) via Cloud KMS
Customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK on disks)
Transparent Data Encryption via the database engine
questions.explanation: Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS let you create, rotate, and control the lifecycle of encryption keys used to protect Cloud SQL data. Google manages the encryption infrastructure, but you control the key. CSEK is used for Compute Engine persistent disks, not Cloud SQL. The default Google-managed keys don't give you key control.

questions.question: You want to containerize a Node.js application and deploy it to Cloud Run using a CI/CD pipeline. Which GCP services would you combine?
options: Cloud Build builds the Docker image, pushes to Artifact Registry, deploys to Cloud Run
App Engine Standard with Cloud Source Repositories triggering an auto-deploy on push
Compute Engine VM with Docker installed and Cloud Scheduler triggering rolling updates
GKE Autopilot with GitOps via Flux and Artifact Registry as the container source
questions.explanation: The standard GCP CI/CD pattern for Cloud Run is: Cloud Build (builds Docker image, runs tests) → Artifact Registry (stores the image) → Cloud Run deployment (gcloud run deploy). Cloud Build triggers can be connected to GitHub/Cloud Source Repositories for automated pipelines.

questions.question: A Kubernetes Deployment has 3 replicas. You apply a new configuration. By default, how does Kubernetes perform the rolling update?
options: Terminates the three old pods first, then creates three new pods together
Creates the three new pods first, then terminates the three old pods together
Replaces pods gradually — one new pod up, one old pod down at a time (RollingUpdate)
Requires a manual approval step before each pod replacement during the rollout
questions.explanation: Kubernetes RollingUpdate strategy (the default) replaces pods incrementally. The default maxUnavailable is 25% and maxSurge is 25%. This means some old pods stay up while new pods come online, maintaining availability throughout the update. You can tune maxSurge/maxUnavailable to balance speed vs availability.

questions.question: You need to migrate a 5 TB PostgreSQL database from on-premises to Cloud SQL with minimal downtime. Which GCP service facilitates this?
options: Cloud Dataflow (Apache Beam jobs)
Database Migration Service (DMS)
Cloud Data Fusion (ETL pipeline)
Transfer Appliance (physical ship)
questions.explanation: Database Migration Service (DMS) provides managed, low-downtime migrations from MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and Oracle to Cloud SQL and AlloyDB. It uses continuous replication to sync changes during migration, minimizing downtime. Dataflow is for data pipeline processing. Data Fusion is ETL/ELT. Transfer Appliance is for offline bulk data transfer.

questions.question: Which GCP product provides a managed Redis or Memcached instance for application caching?
options: Cloud Bigtable
Memorystore
Cloud Datastore
Cloud CDN
questions.explanation: Memorystore is Google Cloud's fully managed in-memory data store service supporting Redis and Memcached. It's used for application caching, session storage, and real-time leaderboards. Cloud CDN caches HTTP content at edge. Bigtable and Datastore are persistent NoSQL databases.

questions.question: After deploying a new version of your app to App Engine, you want to verify it before routing production traffic. What App Engine feature allows this?
options: Deploy the new build to a separate App Engine app in a test project
Use App Engine versions and traffic splitting to send 0% then ramp up
Use a staging service in the same App Engine app fronted by an LB rule
Use Cloud Armor to selectively block production traffic from the new version
questions.explanation: App Engine supports multiple versions of your app simultaneously. You can deploy a new version and allocate 0% of traffic to it, test it by accessing it directly via its version URL (e.g., VERSION-dot-PROJECT.appspot.com), then gradually migrate traffic. This is the standard canary/blue-green pattern in App Engine.

questions.question: What is the maximum size of a single message in Cloud Pub/Sub?
options: 256 KB
1 MB
10 MB
100 MB
questions.explanation: Cloud Pub/Sub supports messages up to 10 MB in size. For larger payloads, the recommended pattern is to store the data in Cloud Storage and publish only a reference (URI) in the Pub/Sub message. This keeps Pub/Sub efficient for event-driven architectures.

questions.question: You need to block all VMs in your organization from having external IP addresses. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Write a Cloud Function that strips external IPs on instance-create events
Apply a VPC firewall rule that blocks all egress at the organization level
Apply an Organization Policy: constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess (deny all)
Configure a Shared VPC without subnets that permit external IP assignment
questions.explanation: The Organization Policy constraint compute.vmExternalIpAccess (or constraints/compute.restrictCloudSQLInstances for SQL) can be set to deny all or allow specific IPs. Applying this at the Organization node cascades down to all folders and projects, preventing any VM from having an external IP. This is the correct governance-level control.

questions.question: Which gcloud command connects you to a Compute Engine VM using OS Login without needing to manage SSH keys manually?
options: gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE_NAME
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa EXTERNAL_IP
gcloud compute connect INSTANCE_NAME
gcloud compute rdp INSTANCE_NAME --ssh
questions.explanation: gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE_NAME handles SSH key management automatically when OS Login is enabled. It pushes your public key to the instance's metadata (or uses OS Login) and connects via IAP TCP tunneling if needed. Manual SSH with a key file requires managing keys yourself.

questions.question: A production GKE cluster must remain highly available if a single GCP zone fails. What cluster configuration achieves this?
options: Single-zone cluster with high-memory nodes and PDBs
Regional cluster with nodes spread across multiple zones
Single-zone cluster with Pod Disruption Budgets enforced
Multi-cluster setup with one cluster per zone per project
questions.explanation: A Regional GKE cluster distributes control plane replicas and node pools across multiple zones (typically 3) within a region. If one zone fails, the cluster continues operating with the remaining zones. Single-zone clusters have a single point of failure. PodDisruptionBudgets manage voluntary disruptions, not zone failures.

questions.question: You need to analyze petabytes of structured data using SQL queries without managing any servers. Which GCP service is the best fit?
options: Cloud Dataproc
Cloud Dataflow
BigQuery
Cloud SQL
questions.explanation: BigQuery is Google's serverless, highly scalable data warehouse. You run SQL queries on petabytes of data and pay per query (or use flat-rate pricing). No infrastructure to manage. Cloud Dataproc is managed Spark/Hadoop. Cloud Dataflow is a stream/batch data pipeline service. Cloud SQL is for OLTP workloads, not petabyte analytics.

questions.question: What is the function of a GKE Ingress resource?
options: Configures NetworkPolicies that govern pod-to-pod traffic in the cluster
Exposes a single backend service externally using an allocated node port
Manages external HTTP(S) access to multiple services via routing rules
Allocates an internal cluster IP for in-cluster service-to-service traffic
questions.explanation: A Kubernetes Ingress resource defines HTTP/HTTPS routing rules (host-based and path-based) and exposes multiple services through a single load balancer IP. On GKE, an Ingress creates a Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancer. Services via NodePort or ClusterIP don't provide the routing flexibility of Ingress.

questions.question: Your team uses Terraform to manage GCP resources. Where should you store the Terraform state file to enable team collaboration and prevent concurrent modification?
options: On each developer's local machine in the working directory
In a Git repository checked in alongside the Terraform code
In a Cloud Storage bucket with versioning and Spanner-based locking
In a Cloud Storage bucket configured as the GCS remote backend
questions.explanation: The GCS (Google Cloud Storage) remote backend stores Terraform state in a bucket, enabling shared access and automatic state locking (using Cloud Storage's atomic operations). This prevents two team members from running terraform apply simultaneously and corrupting state. Local state doesn't support collaboration. Git is not suitable for state files due to sensitive data and concurrent access issues.

questions.question: Which GCP service provides Content Delivery Network (CDN) caching at Google's global edge locations for HTTP(S) load balanced backends?
options: Cloud Armor
Cloud CDN
Cloud Endpoints
Traffic Director
questions.explanation: Cloud CDN integrates with the Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer to cache content at Google's 100+ edge PoPs worldwide, reducing latency and origin load. Cloud Armor provides DDoS protection and WAF. Cloud Endpoints manages APIs. Traffic Director is a managed service mesh control plane.

questions.question: A Cloud Function is failing due to insufficient permissions to write to Cloud Firestore. What is the first thing you should check?
options: Whether the Cloud Functions API is enabled in the project
The IAM role granted to the Cloud Function's service account
Whether the Firestore region matches the Cloud Function region
The memory and CPU allocation set on the Cloud Function
questions.explanation: Cloud Functions run as a service account. By default, this is the App Engine default service account with Editor role, but best practice is to use a dedicated service account with minimal permissions. If a function lacks Firestore write access, the service account needs roles/datastore.user or roles/datastore.owner at minimum.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Cloud Armor and Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)?
options: Cloud Armor handles network-layer DDoS; IAP handles app-layer auth/AuthZ
Cloud Armor is for internal east-west traffic; IAP is for external traffic
IAP supersedes Cloud Armor for app-layer security; Armor is deprecated
Cloud Armor requires GKE backends; IAP integrates with App Engine alone
questions.explanation: Cloud Armor is a WAF/DDoS protection service operating at L3-L7, blocking malicious traffic (SQL injection, XSS, IP blocklists) before it reaches backends. Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) enforces identity-based access control — only authenticated, authorized users can access protected resources. They are complementary, not alternatives.

questions.question: You need to create a custom VPC network for a new project. When creating the VPC, you choose 'Custom' subnet mode. What does this mean?
options: GCP automatically creates one /20 subnet in each region for the VPC
Subnets are created manually with explicit IP ranges (no auto subnets)
The VPC uses IPv6 addressing by default on each subnet created in it
Custom mode allows overlapping IP ranges with other VPCs in the project
questions.explanation: In Custom subnet mode, no subnets are created automatically. You define each subnet's region and CIDR range manually, giving you full control over IP address planning. In Auto mode, GCP creates one /20 subnet per region automatically. Custom mode is recommended for production to avoid overlapping ranges that could prevent future VPC peering.

questions.question: Which command correctly sets the default project and region for all subsequent gcloud commands in a configuration?
options: gcloud set project PROJECT_ID --compute-region=REGION --persist-config
gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID; gcloud config set compute/region REGION
gcloud init --project=PROJECT_ID --compute-region=REGION --skip-prompts
gcloud configure --default-project=PROJECT_ID --default-region=REGION
questions.explanation: gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID sets the active project, and gcloud config set compute/region REGION sets the default Compute Engine region. These can be run separately or chained. gcloud init is interactive and sets up a full configuration. The other options use incorrect flags or syntax.
